entries.title: start release.yml at the tag the release train pushes
entries.body:
* fix(release): start release.yml at the tag the release train pushes

`v0.1.0` was tagged and never built. The tag is on `main`, `CHANGELOG.md`
and `changelog/0.1.0.json` are written, and there is no GitHub release, no
npm tarball and no `nish-0.1.0-x86_64-linux` seed binary — because
`release.yml` has never run, not once.

GitHub raises no event for a ref pushed with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
That is its loop guard, and it has no exemption for ref creation, so
`release.yml`'s `push: tags` trigger never sees a tag `release-pr.yml`
pushed. The comment in `release-pr.yml` claimed otherwise — that pushing
the tag "as a *ref creation*" was enough — and that claim is what broke:
every step succeeded, the notice said "release.yml builds and publishes
it", and nothing built it.

The fix needs no deploy key and no personal access token, because
`workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` are the two events
`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* allowed to raise. `release-pr.yml` now pushes the tag
and then dispatches `release.yml` at it, under a new `actions: write`
permission. The ref carries through as `GITHUB_REF_NAME`, which is what
every step of `release.yml` already reads, so a dispatched run and a
human's `git push origin v0.1.0` build the same thing from the same lines.
The `push: tags` trigger stays for the human case — which is also how a
tag stranded by this bug is recovered.

Two guards, because the failure mode here was silence rather than red.
`gh workflow run` returning 0 means the dispatch was accepted, not that a
run exists, so the step polls for the run and says which it got: a notice
when it sees one, and a warning naming the one command that finishes the
job when it does not. A dispatch that is actually refused fails the step
outright. And `release.yml` now checks `GITHUB_REF_TYPE` before it
compares versions, so a dispatch aimed at a branch reports the mis-aimed
run it is instead of a version mismatch.

`release.yml` also gains a concurrency group keyed on the ref. Two ways in
means two ways to land on one tag; serialising means the second run fails
honestly at `gh release create` rather than racing the first through a
half-published release.

Recovering 0.1.0 is one manual push, because the `v0.1.0` tag points at a
commit whose `release.yml` predates this one and therefore has no
`workflow_dispatch` trigger to aim at.

Refs: docs/wp12-release.md, docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md#g3
Tests: node docs/check-links.mjs; both workflows parse; the dispatch,
  poll-success, poll-timeout and refused-dispatch paths exercised against
  a stub `gh`

* perf(tests): compare the stage0 oracles in parallel, and batch self/'s compile gate

`npm test` is 19m29s of CI's 20m26s, and half of it is the self-hosting
section. Two checks account for 390s of that — a third of the entire run —
and both are the same shape: the whole corpus through *both* compilers, one
program at a time, on a runner with four cores sitting idle.

Every program those oracles compare is independent of every other — two
compilers, one input, a directory each — so they now run `--jobs` at a time,
one job per core and capped at eight. The cap is memory rather than
politeness: each job holds a whole module graph, and a 64-core runner forking
64 compilers is how a suite gets OOM-killed instead of getting faster.

`pool` already existed for the WP13 differential runner and already kept the
input order, so it moves to `tests/pool.js` with a promise-shaped `spawn`
beside it rather than being written a second time;
`tests/differential/lib.js` imports it from there and keeps re-exporting it,
so the runners that import it from there are unchanged.

**Order is what makes this safe, and it is checked rather than asserted.**
Each result is written into the slot its input came from and the summaries
are walked in corpus order, so every count and every named failure is what a
sequential run produced. Both oracles were run `--jobs 1 --verbose` and again
at the default width: the output is byte-identical, every verbose skip,
negative and dump line included.

  checked_oracle.js   141.0 s -> 49.0 s   325/325 files, 308,384 dump lines
  ir_oracle.js        172.4 s -> 54.9 s   334/334 programs, 2,389,591 IR lines

`--jobs 1` is the sequential runner these used to be, and is the first thing
to reach for when a parallel run says something surprising.

The third cost was repetition rather than serialism. The gate that proves
stage0 accepts every module of `self/` compiled each of the 58 modules as its
own root: 58 process starts and 58 walks of the module graph to prove one
thing. Named together they are one walk. The four entry points are compiled
apart from the rest because only the entry module may declare `export
function main`, and they are found the way `scripts/smoke.sh` finds them,
both spellings. A green batch reports the same 58 checks under the same
names; a red one falls back to the per-module loop so a failure is still
attributed to a module rather than dumped as a wall of text — checked against
a deliberately broken module, which the fallback names with its own
diagnostic.

  self/ compile gate   45.6 s -> 5.1 s

Both oracles now set `process.exitCode` instead of calling `process.exit`:
stdout is a pipe when `tests/run.js` spawns them, writes to a pipe are
asynchronous, and `process.exit` does not wait for them. The summary is the
whole result, so losing its tail to a forced exit would read as an oracle
that said nothing.

Read the ratios against the core count. These were measured on four cores,
where the two oracles come out a little over 3x; the GitHub runner reports
two (`differential` prints `2 jobs` there and `4 jobs` here), so CI should
see about half of the oracle saving and all of the compile gate's -- roughly
19m30s to 15m30s for the `Test` step rather than the 3x the numbers below
would suggest on their own.

Measured: npm test 15m55s -> 12m21s, 1223 passed / 0 failed / 2 skipped both
  times; checked_oracle 141.0s -> 49.0s, ir_oracle 172.4s -> 54.9s, the self/
  compile gate 45.6s -> 5.1s, on 4 cores
Refs: .claude/selfhost.md, docs/wp14-selfhost.md
Tests: npm test, 1223 passed 0 failed 2 skipped -- the same counts and the
  same two skips as before the change; both oracles diffed --jobs 1 against
  the default width over the whole corpus (byte-identical, verbose included);
  the batch gate's fallback against a deliberately broken module; pool order
  preserved under randomised completion
